ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: Climbing a tree to seek fish marks effort directed where its object cannot be found.
EvidenceBody: Fenyang, Jingyin, Yongming, and Kaifu use the image in verse and instruction; Zhongfeng develops it in his own exposition, while Qingshan applies it to the Yunju–Dongshan encounter.

DraftEvidence.ZenBend: The tree and fish belong to incompatible domains, which is why Chan records use the image for effort whose chosen route cannot reach its goal.
DraftEvidence.CounterexampleOrLimit: The idiom marks pursuing an object by means incapable of attaining it.

ComparedThings: to climb a tree seeking fish
the retained dialogue, sermon, verse, and appraisal uses
DifferentThingTest.Reason: Verse, hall warning, and doctrinal preface retain one impossibility: climbing wood never becomes a way to fish.

DraftEvidence.AliasRationale: The alias names both the attempted climb and its unattainable catch.

ModifierControls.Finding: 緣木 supplies the misdirected approach and 求魚 its desired object; neither half alone carries the idiom.

FamilyControls.Finding: The neighboring stump-and-hare proverb shares futility but remains a separate image and entry.
